For Claude Code, Skills seem to overlap heavily with the existing practice of listing markdown 'guides' in CLAUDE.md. Skills may simply make managing those guides more organized and declarative.
A user who has been having Claude Code create and organize skills says they can have diminishing returns.
A user sees it as a big downside to have more and more provider-specific features like Skills: more to learn, more to configure, and more to get locked into.
A user who has been burned building vendor-locked chatbot extensions prefers to wait until this stabilizes or is standardized before writing a 'skill' against an actual RFC or standard protocol.

Skills are 'like MCPs on demand.' One user switched several MCP servers to plain scripts because the servers were eating about 20% of the context just by being there. Now the model reads and uses a script only when needed.

Skeptic: Skills don't add much to a Claude Code workflow that already uses specialized agents and a custom MCP for searching indexed docs. 'Skills' is also a bad name, since it's really a selective context-loading system for hierarchical docs.

A user already ran a 'Table of Contents' approach, linking specialized docs from CLAUDE.md without '@' so they don't bloat the context. They see Skills as an iterative formalization rather than a breakthrough, and plan to swap over to see if the official version works better.

If you've worked with Excel + Python, the xlsx SKILL.md in github.com/anthropics/skills shows the value: there are many edge cases in reading and writing Excel files with Python, and it 'nails many of them.'
Complaint: if Skills are meant to be efficient for LLMs, structured schemas like JSON would be better. Markdown is a happy medium for humans, but it's non-deterministic to parse.

Skills don't replace MCP. A skill is a markdown and YAML file on your filesystem, while an MCP server is accessed over HTTP and can handle user auth. MCP can also be fully server-side, so average users don't have to manage local skill files or run Python scripts locally.

Months of experimenting with skills changed how one user thinks about LLMs: agents are a user of the product, not a feature. When a skill fails on internal tools, it's often the tools' fault: bad docs and opaque API errors. Fixing these for the LLM also helps human users.

Several users report agents don't invoke skills without being asked. One finds skills aren't triggered by expected keywords and has to call them explicitly. Another has 'an incredibly hard time' getting skills used at all, even when asked.

Even with proper YAML headers, semantic triggers, and a short, specific list of skills, one user must be very specific to trigger a skill. It's hit or miss, and they usually have to say 'there is a skill for this, go use it.'

Citing Vercel's evals: the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases, and adding it gave no improvement over baseline. AGENTS.md gave broad improvements, while skills worked better for vertical, explicitly triggered workflows.

Workaround: putting the skill's instructions directly in the general AGENTS.md 'works just fine.' Another user has AGENTS.md explicitly point to the repo's skill directory, keeps few skills, and updates a skill whenever the agent goes off script.

Advice from experience: people put way too much into claude.md files and skills. Keep top-level context as 'information about information.' Make skills light-touch instructions for scripts, APIs, and MCPs, and trim anything Claude already knows; Claude itself pads these files.

A developer liked the Skills architecture but ran workloads on Gemini 2.5 Flash, so they built a model-agnostic version adapted from github.com/anthropics/skills. They found cold starts slow with very large package sets and 15+ Skills.
